### Principle 1: Shared Company Culture and Values

#### Depth: Communicating Across Levels

Designing with data diminishes reliance on “gut” decision making and can break hierarchical structures. Company-wide data literacy—addressing well-formulated, carefully investigated questions using techniques like A/B testing, ethnographic field research, field deployments, surveys, lab studies, and usability research—invites discussion, challenge, and the possibility of being wrong. Such grounded and carefully gathered user data drives decisions and is less risky than relying on executive “gut feelings.”

An early 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield (“Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO”) addressed this. HIPPO stands for Highest Paid Person’s Opinion. The principle: data resolves conflicts without relying on rank, hierarchy, or company politics. John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix, explained that data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation, creating a non-political environment: “everyone knew that the best person with the best data would win out.”

Patty McCord, former Chief Talent Officer at Netflix (over 12 years), described a key mechanism: “If you don’t have the mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for your customers, the only person who’s going to be able to say yay or nay is the person at the highest level of the organization.” Without such a mechanism, decisions default to the single highest-ranking individual. Having an objective measurement allows more people to have a voice in product development, freeing the company from reliance on a single decision-maker.

Netflix’s data-driven approach succeeded because the practice was well established and universally accepted throughout the company—it may have started at the top with CEO Reed Hastings and CPO Neil Hunt driving and believing in the value, but it was also embraced by everyone through management to individual contributors. McCord explained that at Netflix, even the CEO cannot simply do what he wants. Any employee, including executives, can get caught up in thinking they know the answer. A/B testing mitigates top-down problem solving because everyone can learn from experimentation, and being wrong becomes a learning opportunity.

When Reed Hastings had a strong product idea, he submitted it to the same A/B testing rigor as everyone else. On rare occasions he might dictate exact implementation, but only on “his test cell”—the experimental group he was backing, tested against other cells proposed by the product team. If it didn’t win, it wasn’t launched. Having upper management hold themselves accountable to the same process reinforced subjecting ideas, prototypes, features, and flows to grounded review through experimentation, and accepting “failure” as a positive outcome—this value was central to how the company should work.

To shift into a data-aware framework, examine how product and design decisions have been made to date. If decisions were concentrated in one or two individuals, ensure they recognize the value of bringing in user/customer data, as their individual weight will diminish. The authors advise checking your own comfort as well: are you also willing to see how incorporating data will change the weight of your own opinion within the design and product development process?

# Appendix C: Statistical Methods Used in Our Research

## Source Content

The source text for Appendix C consists solely of a bibliography. No statistical methods, analytical procedures, or methodological descriptions are presented in the provided text. The bibliography serves as a reference list for the statistical approaches and supporting literature used elsewhere in the book.

## Bibliographic Content

The bibliography contains 86 references spanning multiple disciplines relevant to the research. These include:

- **DevOps and continuous delivery**: Humble & Farley (2010), Kim et al. (2016), Behr et al. (2004)
- **Organizational culture**: Westrum (2004), Schein (1985), Pettigrew (1979)
- **Lean and agile methods**: Ries (2013), Blank (2013), Beck et al. (2001)
- **Statistical methodology**: Hair et al. (2006) for multivariate data analysis; Brown (2006) for confirmatory factor analysis; Chin (2010) and Chin et al. (2003) for partial least squares (PLS) analysis; Nunnally (1978) for psychometric theory
- **Validation guidelines**: Straub et al. (2004) and Gefen & Straub (2005) for IS positivist research validation
- **Common method variance assessment**: Lindell & Whitney (2001), Podsakoff & Dalton (1987)
- **Burnout and engagement**: Maslach & Leiter (2008), Leiter & Maslach (2008), Chandola et al. (2006)
- **Team diversity and performance**: Woolley & Malone (2011), Rock & Grant (2016), Google (2015)
- **Resilience engineering**: ACMQueue (2012), Perrow (2011)
- **Leadership and culture**: Rafferty & Griffin (2004), Stone et al. (2004), Shook (2010)
- **Product development flow**: Reinertsen (2009)
- **Lean enterprise**: Humble et al. (2014)
- **Salary surveys**: SAGE (2008, 2012), King & Magoulas (2016)
- **Industry reports**: Deloitte (2013), Forrester (2017), Gartner (2016), IDC (2014)

Key statistical references include foundational works on PLS analysis (Chin et al. 2003; Chin 2010), confirmatory factor analysis (Brown 2006), and common method variance assessment (Lindell & Whitney 2001; Podsakoff & Dalton 1987). The bibliography also cites research on burnout and engagement (Maslach & Leiter 2008; Leiter & Maslach 2008), team diversity (Woolley & Malone 2011; Rock & Grant 2016), and resilience engineering (ACMQueue 2012; Perrow 2011). Additional references cover working memory (Alloway & Alloway 2013), automation and jobs (Bessen 2017), and organizational classification (Ulrich & McKelvey 1990).

## Caveat

The absence of statistical methods description means the summary cannot provide any explanatory detail about the analytical techniques, conceptual distinctions, mechanisms, or examples that would normally appear in a methods appendix. The bibliography serves as a reference list for the statistical approaches used elsewhere in the book but does not itself contain methodological content. Readers must consult the cited works (e.g., Hair et al. 2006, Brown 2006, Chin 2010) for details on the specific statistical procedures employed. The bibliography does not indicate which methods were used for which analyses, nor does it explain the rationale for methodological choices. This is a limitation of the source text for this appendix.
